newsitem.title: USA: Taxes high on Indiana legislative agenda.
newsitem.headline: Taxes high on Indiana legislative agenda.

text.p: Taxes will be on the minds of some Indiana lawmakers returning to session on Tuesday.
In the Democrat-controlled House, members will be eyeing targeted tax cuts, according to Steve Jackson, assistant director of media relations for Democrat representatives.

With a record combined fiscal 1996 balance of $1.68 billion, House Democrats will propose the elimination of text book rental fees for public school students, an increase to $2,000 from $1,000 in the state income tax deduction for dependents under 18, and a college tuition tax credit of up to $5,000 per year, per child, Jackson said.
He said thost and other tax proposals will come up in conjunction with a fiscal 1998-99 budget.

The Nov. 5 election resulted in a 50-50 split between Democrats and Republicans in the House, with the Democrats gaining control of the chamber through a 1995 state law that turns control over to the party of the governor. Lt. Gov. Frank O'Bannon, a Democrat, won the race for governor over Indianapolis Mayor Stephen Goldsmith.

Another matter lawmakers in both the House and Senate might address is the state's method of assessing property taxes. The Indiana Supreme Court last month overturned a state tax court ruling that found the system to be unconstitutional because it was not based solely on fair market valuation. The high court also vacated a March 1998 deadline for the state to fix the current system and returned the case to the tax court to determine whether the current system results in non-uniform and unequal property valuations.
"That removed the gun from our heads," Jackson said. "But it doesn't mean the issue will go away."
He said there was still impetus to address "some aspects of the system."
Gretchen Gutman, fiscal analyst for the Republican majority in the Indiana Senate, said bills addressing the administration of the property tax system are expected to be introduced.
The Senate will also be looking at the school funding formula as part of the biennial budget, Gutman said.

Another big ticket item in the budget will be corrections. Gutman said that the state department of corrections will ask for $247 million to build three prisons. Lawmakers will decide whether to approve the plan and if the prisons should be funded with cash or with lease-revenue bonds, she added.
